segments.heading: File header: what the self-test checks, and its limits
segments.text:
- The comment states the method. Each kernel runs on a buffer that lies between two pages with no access rights (guard pages). The program compares the memory afterwards.
- `PROT_NONE` is the protection value that forbids every access to a page. `SIGSEGV` is the signal that the Linux kernel sends to a process on a forbidden memory access. It ends the process.
- The limits matter for the review. The test cannot show that a read kernel loads all the bytes of its buffer. The machine code listing is the evidence for that [Ref3].
- Callee-saved registers are registers that a function must restore before it returns. The test does not check them.

segments.heading: Include the benchmark source itself
segments.text:
- `#include "bandwidth.c"` copies the whole text of bandwidth.c into this file. The compiler looks for it in the folder of selftest.c first. That file is the new benchmark source, the one that bw_new is built from [Ref1].
- The six kernels are `static` functions of bandwidth.c. The include makes them callable from this file.
- The `#define` renames the `main` function of bandwidth.c to `bandwidth_main` while the include is read. `#undef` ends the renaming. Nothing calls `bandwidth_main`.
- bandwidth.c also includes the system headers that this file needs.
`page` holds the page size in bytes. `main` sets it (line 143). `failures` counts the checks that failed.

segments.heading: Function `guarded`: a buffer between two guard pages
segments.text:
- `mmap` reserves `len` bytes plus two pages. `PROT_NONE` forbids every access to all of it. `MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS` means memory of this process only. It is not the content of a file.
- `mprotect` then allows reads and writes for the `len` bytes that start one page after the start of the mapping. The page before them and the page after them stay forbidden. These are the two guard pages.
- The function returns the address of the first byte after the front guard page.
- If `mmap` or `mprotect` fails, the program prints the error and ends with exit status 2.
- `n * 8` must be a multiple of the page size. Then the last byte of the buffer is the last byte before the rear guard page.

segments.heading: Function `pattern`: the test value of word `i`
segments.text:
- Returns `(i + 1)` times a fixed 64-bit constant, then XOR (bitwise exclusive or, `^`) with `salt`.
- The constant is odd. Two different indexes therefore never give the same value for the same `salt`.
- The file has four fill loops (lines 63, 84, 111 and 120). They pass the salts 1 to 4. So no two fills give a word the same value.

segments.heading: Function `calling`: the line printed before a kernel call
segments.text: Prints `call,<kernel name>,<bytes>`. `n` is a count of 8-byte words. `n * 8` is the byte count. If the kernel call then ends the process with `SIGSEGV`, this is the last line of the output, and it names the kernel.

segments.heading: Function `check`: one result line
segments.text: Prints one result line: kernel name, name of the check, byte count, then `pass` or `FAIL`. A failed check adds 1 to `failures`. The program continues after a failed check.

Three types of pointer to a kernel function, one per kind of kernel. A read kernel takes a buffer and a word count. A write kernel also takes the value to store. A copy kernel takes the destination, the source and the word count.

segments.heading: Function `test_size`: read, write and copy over a whole buffer
segments.text:
- `n` is the buffer size in 8-byte words.
- `rn`, `wn` and `cn` are the names that the output shows for the read, write and copy kernel. `rd`, `wr` and `cp` are the kernel functions.
- Line 58 gets two guarded buffers `a` and `b` of `n` words each.

- Fill `a` with the pattern of salt 1.
- Print the `call` line. Then run the read kernel once over the whole buffer.
- Compare every word with the pattern. `ok` stays 1 only when all `n` words equal the pattern.
- The buffer fills the space between the two guard pages exactly. A load up to one page before its first byte, or up to one page after its last byte, ends the process.
- The check passes also when the kernel loads nothing. It cannot show that every byte was loaded.

- `v` is the value to store. It depends on `n`, so each buffer size uses another value.
- Run the write kernel once over the whole buffer `a`.
- Every word must equal `v` afterwards. A word that the kernel did not write keeps its old value from the read test, and the check fails.

- Fill the source `a` with the pattern of salt 2. Fill the destination `b` with zeros.
- Run the copy kernel once: `cp(b, a, n)` copies `n` words from `a` to `b`.
- First check: every word of `b` equals the pattern. No two words of the source hold the same value. A store of the wrong value or to the wrong offset therefore fails the check.
- Second check: `a` still holds the pattern.
Release both buffers together with their guard pages. Each mapping starts one page before the buffer and is two pages longer than the buffer.

segments.heading: Function `test_block`: one 256 B loop pass inside one page
segments.text:
- `a` and `b` are guarded buffers of one page each (`n` words). `m` is 32 words (256 B). That is the amount that one loop pass of each kernel moves [Ref6].
- `off` is the word offset of the 256 B block inside the page. `main` passes 0 (block at the page start, directly after the front guard page) and `page / 8 - 32` (block at the page end, directly before the rear guard page).
- Each kernel is called for exactly these 32 words. A correct kernel runs one loop pass and returns.

- Fill the page `a` with the pattern of salt 3.
- Run the read kernel on the 32 words at `a + off`.
- The whole page must be unchanged.
- Block at the page start: a load before the block reads the front guard page, and the process ends.
- Block at the page end: a load after the block (a second loop pass, for example) reads the rear guard page, and the process ends.
- The text of the check says `page start` when `off` is 0, and `page end` otherwise.

- Fill the page `b` with the pattern of salt 4.
- Run the copy kernel: 32 words from `a + off` to `b + off`.
- Expected in `b`: the 32 words of the block hold the values of `a` (salt 3). All other words still hold the pattern of salt 4.
- A store next to the block changes one of those other words, or it writes to a guard page.

- Run the write kernel: store `v` to the 32 words at `a + off`.
- Expected in `a`: the 32 words of the block equal `v`. All other words still hold the pattern of salt 3.
- The order in this function is read, copy, write. The copy check (line 125) expects that the source `a` still holds the pattern of salt 3. The write test changes `a`, so it runs last.
Release both pages together with their guard pages.

segments.heading: Function `main`: run all checks and report
segments.text:
- The program takes no arguments.
- `setvbuf` with `_IOLBF` makes the standard output line-buffered: each line is written out as soon as it is complete. run_kernels.sh sends the output to a file [Ref1]. Without this call the lines would stay in a memory buffer of the process, and they would be lost when a `SIGSEGV` ends the process.
- `sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE)` returns the page size in bytes. It was 4096 bytes on CRB [Ref2].
- Line 144 prints the header line: the page size and the column names of the result lines.
- The kernels move 256 B per loop pass. If the page size is not a multiple of 256 B, the program ends with exit status 2.

- Three buffer sizes in words: 1 page, 3 pages and 1 MiB. With 4096-byte pages these are 512, 1536 and 131072 words.
- For each size `test_size` runs twice. The first run tests the C kernels `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy`. The second run tests the asm kernels `k_asmread`, `k_asmwrite` and `k_asmcopy`.
- The strings are the names in the output. `read` is `k_read`, the new read kernel.

- Two word offsets: 0 (page start) and `page / 8 - 32` (the last 32 words of the page, word 480 with 4096-byte pages).
- For each offset `test_block` runs twice: C kernels first, then asm kernels.

Print the number of failed checks. Exit status 0 means that every check passed. Exit status 1 means that at least one check failed. run_kernels.sh stops before its timed runs when the status is not 0 [Ref1].
